extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Horace / scholars of classical Latin literature; translators and teachers of Roman satire
extracted.subtask_description: Reading, annotating, and evaluating Horace's Satires and Epistles with attention to authorial technique, thematic aims (ethical/philosophical instruction), use of verisimilitude, rhetorical devices, and moral messaging. Includes commentary on specific passages (dinner-party satire, didactic epistle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Securing verisimilitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Securing a certain amount of verisimilitude through the use of known facts, and of drawing on his imagination for the rest of his material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use real, identifiable facts or social conventions (arrangement of couches, named guests, culinary customs) to ground a satirical scene so that invented details seem plausible; combine documented detail with imaginative invention to achieve credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid heaping ridicule on a real host who offered hospitality
rubrics_metrics.description: These facts warrant us in acquitting Fundanius (and therefore the author who introduced him) on the charge of extremely bad taste in heaping ridicule on a host whose hospitality had been accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When satirising social situations, take care about ridiculing identifiable, real hosts who provided hospitality; contextualize or fictionalize to avoid impropriety and preserve verisimilitude without unethical exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target selection for satire (subjects)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Satire is directed, partly against the ostentation and vulgarity sometimes displayed by wealth, and partly against the curious and affected erudition of pronounced epicures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose behaviours or social types that lend themselves to moral/social critique (e.g., ostentation, affected taste). Make the satirical target clear by focusing on characteristic excesses and pretensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of vivid material detail for comedic/satirical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed descriptions of foods, sauces, wines, slaves' actions, and mishaps (canopy falling, broken dishes) underscore the satire of ostentation and the comic fallout of extravagance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ concrete, sensory particulars (culinary ingredients, table-servants, gestures) to dramatize folly and to produce comic contrast between appearance and reality; specificity enhances both realism and ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize novelty over mere badness in satirical depiction of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: The point lies, not in the badness, but in the novelty, of the dishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To satirize gastronomic affectation, foreground eccentricity/novelty and the guests' pretensions rather than simply claiming the food is bad; show how novelty becomes a status marker and occasion for ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitative sound devices to mirror action
rubrics_metrics.description: The remarkable accumulation of sibilants in l. 78 imitates the whispering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use phonetic and sonic devices (sibilance, alliteration) purposefully to mimic or evoke actions and atmospheres (e.g., whispering), reinforcing the scene's mood and enhancing comic or rhetorical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staging and arrangement to characterize social relations
rubrics_metrics.description: The party was arranged according to the following plan: (list of seating positions). Positions on couches (above/below, middle couch) identify status and behaviours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage scenes with attention to spatial relationships (seating order, who sits near whom) as a means of characterizing hierarchy, complicity, and comic contrast among participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal character through mishaps/adversity
rubrics_metrics.description: One who entertains is like a general: mishaps oft reveal his genius, smooth going hides it. (aulaea falling, servants' blunders reveal host's temperament)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let incidents and small disasters expose hosts' or characters' underlying qualities (vanity, panic, magnanimity); use trouble to disclose rather than simply to amuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dialogic persona and interlocutor
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace frames episodes as dialogue (Horace with Davus, Fundanius) to present scenes and moral points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt dramatic dialogue with named interlocutors to present events, allow differing perspectives, and let moral or comic judgments emerge organically from speech rather than direct authorial preaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of ethical/philosophical didacticism
rubrics_metrics.description: The Epistle professes to explain why Horace has given up lyric poetry; it advances Stoic/Cyrenaic reflections: 'The first step in virtue and wisdom is to eschew vice and folly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing epistles or didactic poetry, integrate moral instruction with personal anecdote and philosophical exempla; make remedies or 'cures' for vice concrete and practicable (rules, analogies, spells).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of exempla and classical allusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace uses exempla (fox declining lion's den) and references to Plato, Aristotle, Simonides to illustrate points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ brief illustrative stories and authoritative allusions to classical figures to condense argument, legitimize stance, and provide mnemonic/analogical force; ensure the exemplum supports the ethical or comic point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial stance: measured eclecticism (not bound to one school)
rubrics_metrics.description: I am not bound to swear to the words of any master; now behaving as a true Stoic..., and now relapsing into the passiveness of a Cyrenaic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a flexible, conversational persona that can draw on multiple philosophical positions; this allows the writer to explore tensions and maintain rhetorical balance rather than doctrinaire certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and planning of material for future use
rubrics_metrics.description: I am putting by and setting in order the stores on which I may some day draw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and arrange material consciously: set aside verses/notes and assemble a repertory of scenes, examples, and reflections to be deployed later; disciplined compilation aids sustained composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral messaging: virtue prioritized over wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is to flee vice and wisdom is to have got rid of folly... 'Of less worth than gold is silver, than virtue gold.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that ethical themes are woven into the text's argumentative spine: contrast external markers of success (wealth, novelty) with inner goods (virtue, self-control) and make the moral preference clear through exemplification rather than mere assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of irony and restraint in tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace often balances mockery with sympathetic philosophical reflection; e.g., he notes his own faults alongside those he ridicules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ self-awareness and ironic distance in satire and didactic pieces: allow the narrator to acknowledge personal inconsistency to prevent purely punitive ridicule and to invite reader reflection.
